I’m a 33-year-old farmer with five years under my belt here in Quzhou County, and I’ve learned that you can’t chase every fad. My land is 163 mu, my household has four mouths, and two of us work off-farm part of the year, so labor is tight. Well irrigation is my lifeline on the North China Plain, but water and time still cost money.

Here is my thinking. The backbone of my farm is the wheat–maize double crop. That rotation fits our climate and soil perfectly, and with the grain subsidies and reliable buyers, it’s my safest income. I’ll dedicate 120 mu to it—winter wheat followed by summer maize. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because the yield jump pays for itself. For the remaining 43 mu, I need cash crops that match my labor limits. I’ll plant 15 mu of watermelon in spring; it brings good money at the county market and is done by midsummer before the maize harvest rush. Cotton is low-intensity day-to-day, so I’ll put 15 mu there—it runs through summer into autumn and doesn’t need the constant hand-work that vegetables do. I’ll do 8 mu of broccoli in autumn on a corner plot after the early crops come off; it sells well to the cooperatives. Five mu of chili gives me dried-fallback value if fresh prices drop. Finally, I’ll trial 3 mu of stevia—a buyer promised a contract last year, and I’m willing to risk a small patch. I rotary-till most fields to save time, but I plough the wheat land properly to bury residue and level the seedbed. Fertilizer follows what the extension station recommends: heavier nitrogen for the grains, extra potassium for the melons and chili, and moderate doses all around. I spray pesticides only when I see pests, but cotton and melon need more vigilance.
